title: Conditional Probability
intro: After this lesson you can recognize a conditional probability, write it with the vertical bar, compute it from a table or with $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$, and use the general multiplication rule and tree diagrams.

moments.title: Conditional probability
moments.text: The probability that $A$ occurs given that $B$ has occurred, written $P(A\mid B)$.

moments.title: Condition goes after the bar
moments.text: In words the condition can sit anywhere. In notation it always follows the vertical bar.

moments.title: Home-team fans and food
moments.text: Marginal, joint and conditional questions from the same two-way table of 250 people.

moments.title: Conditional probability formula
moments.text: $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$. The condition goes on the bottom.

moments.title: The formula matches the table
moments.text: Dividing $120/250$ by $160/250$ cancels the 250s and gives $120/160$.

moments.title: Turkey and ham at Thanksgiving
moments.text: 72% have turkey, 21% ham and 11% neither. Fill a table to get $P(\text{ham}\mid\text{turkey})$.

moments.title: Spot conditional statements in words
moments.text: "If ... then the probability that" and "given that" both signal a condition.

moments.title: Two green marbles
moments.text: $\frac{4}{20}\cdot\frac{3}{19}$, because the condition removes one green marble.

moments.title: Netflix and Disney Plus table
moments.text: Restrict to the 180 Netflix subscribers, then count those who also have Disney Plus.

moments.title: Tree diagrams
moments.text: Branches show conditional probabilities. The end of each path is a joint probability.

moments.title: Defective light bulbs
moments.text: Add the two paths that end in "defective": $0.6(0.04)+0.4(0.10)=0.064$.

moments.title: Disease and test result
moments.text: With a rare disease, $P(\text{disease}\mid\text{positive})\approx0.107$ even though the test is 95% sensitive.

cards.name: Marginal
cards.text: One event. Use the table total as the denominator.

cards.name: Joint
cards.text: "A and B". Use $P(A)\cdot P(B\mid A)$ or a cell over the table total.

cards.name: Conditional
cards.text: "Given", "if", "of those". Divide by the probability or count of the condition.

cells: What is the probability a fan purchased food?
What is the probability a fan roots for the home team and buys food?
Given that a fan bought food, what is the probability the fan roots for the home team?
If a person has turkey, what is the probability of ham?
A bulb is from machine B and is defective
A bulb is defective. What is the probability it came from machine B?

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The video names the denominators in words. On the exam, write the probability statement, such as $P(\text{B}\mid\text{defective})$, before you substitute numbers.

sections.title: Use a tree diagram
sections.intro: Start with the first split, add the conditional probabilities on each second branch, multiply along a path for a joint probability, and add paths for a total.
steps: Draw the first split and label each branch with its probability.
On each branch, draw the second split with conditional probabilities.
Multiply along a path for a joint probability with the general multiplication rule.
Add the paths that match the event to get its total, then divide to reverse the condition.

parts.label: Positive
parts.text: $P(\text{disease}\mid\text{positive})$. Few have the disease, so most positives are false.

traps.title: Adding conditional probabilities
traps.better: Multiply each conditional probability by the probability of its branch, then add: $0.6(0.04)+0.4(0.10)=0.064$.

traps.title: Reversing the condition
traps.weak: $P(\text{positive}\mid\text{disease})=0.95$, so a positive test means a 95% chance of disease.
traps.better: $P(\text{disease}\mid\text{positive})=0.0095/0.0887\approx0.107$. The two conditional probabilities are different.

traps.title: Show the probability statement
traps.better: $P(\text{machine B}\mid\text{defective})=\dfrac{0.4(0.10)}{0.064}=0.625$. About 62.5% of defective bulbs come from machine B.

traps.title: Forgetting the changed denominator
traps.better: After one green marble is removed, $P(\text{green}\mid\text{green first})=3/19$, so the product is $\frac{4}{20}\cdot\frac{3}{19}\approx0.032$.

traps.title: Interpreting a conditional probability
traps.weak: 25% of students are in science club, so a math club member has a 25% chance.
traps.better: $P(\text{science}\mid\text{math})=0.12/0.30=0.40$. Knowing a student is in math club raises the chance to 40%, above the overall 25%.

questions.stem: Among 200 students, 80 own a bike and 50 own a skateboard; 30 own both. What is $P(\text{skateboard}\mid\text{bike})$?
why: Correct. Divide the joint count by the bike owners: $30/80=0.375$.
This is $P(\text{bike}\mid\text{skateboard})$, with the condition reversed.
This is the marginal probability of owning a skateboard.

questions.stem: A box has 5 red and 7 blue pens. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
why: Probabilities of consecutive events are multiplied, not added.
This is the probability of red then blue.
This treats the draws as independent with replacement.

questions.stem: On a team, 60% of players are guards and 40% are forwards. A guard makes 50% of free throws; a forward makes 70%. What is $P(\text{a random player makes a free throw})$?
why: Adding 0.5 and 0.7 does not weight by group size.
This is the probability a player is a guard.
This uses only the guards free throw percentage.

opts: The probability that $A$ and $B$ both occur
The probability that $A$ occurs given that $B$ has occurred
The probability that $B$ occurs given that $A$ has occurred
why: Correct. The event after the vertical bar is the condition.

sections.title: Free-response practice
sections.prompt: A website records that 55% of visitors use a mobile device and 45% use a desktop. Of mobile visitors, 8% make a purchase. Of desktop visitors, 14% make a purchase.
parts: (a) Draw a tree diagram, or describe it, labeling each branch.
(b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen visitor makes a purchase.
(c) A visitor made a purchase. Find the probability that the visitor used a mobile device.
(d) Is a desktop visitor more likely to purchase than a randomly chosen visitor? Justify.
sample: (a) First branches: mobile 0.55, desktop 0.45. From mobile: purchase 0.08, no purchase 0.92. From desktop: purchase 0.14, no purchase 0.86.
(d) Yes. $P(\text{purchase}\mid\text{desktop})=0.14$, which is greater than the overall 0.107.
checklist: (d) Compares 0.14 to the overall purchase rate
